questions.question_text: Differentiate $y = 3x\sin x$ using the product rule.

options.why: Multiplied the two derivatives together instead of using the product rule.
Used the subtraction of the quotient rule inside a product.
Differentiated only the trigonometric factor and left $3x$ unchanged.

questions.solution_text:
$u = 3x, \quad u' = 3$
$v = \sin x, \quad v' = \cos x$
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3(\sin x) + 3x(\cos x)$
$= 3\sin x + 3x\cos x$

This is $(\sin x)^{2}$, whose derivative is $2\sin x\cos x$.
The $2$ multiplies $x$ rather than squaring it, so the derivative is $2\cos 2x$.
Differentiating cosine gives a negative sine, so the derivative is $-2x\sin(x^{2})$.
